## 2

I understand why you're skeptical of big institutions and government agencies, but the evidence for a curved Earth doesn't rely on NASA or digital images. People figured out the planet's shape thousands of years before cameras existed.

Think about everyday observations that anyone can verify: 
- Ships don't shrink into a dot as they sail away; their hulls disappear over the horizon before their masts do. 
- During a lunar eclipse, the shadow the Earth casts onto the Moon is always circular, regardless of the Earth's angle, which only a sphere can do. 
- You can buy your own telescope and watch the rotation of Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn, or look at how the visible constellations completely change when you travel between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

If millions of people across centuries—from ancient navigators and amateur astronomers to commercial pilots and telecommunications engineers worldwide—were part of a cover-up, it would be the most complex, leak-proof conspiracy in human history, without any clear motive. Why do you find that more likely than the planet simply being round?

## 3

Sunlight looks plain white to us, but it’s actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow combined together. 

You can think of light traveling in waves. Red light travels in long, lazy waves, while blue light travels in short, choppy, energetic waves.

When sunlight hits Earth, it has to pass through our atmosphere, which is packed with billions of tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). The longer wavelengths, like red and yellow, mostly pass straight through those molecules without bumping into them. But because blue light has those short, choppy waves, it constantly collides with the gas particles and bounces off in every single direction. This process is called *Rayleigh scattering*.

When you look up during the day, you’re seeing all that scattered blue light bouncing down into your eyes from every corner of the sky. 

(And if you're wondering: violet light actually scatters even more than blue, but the Sun produces a lot more blue light to begin with, and our human eyes happen to be much more sensitive to blue than violet.)
